title: Dungeon Dive Hobbycast - Episode 3 - Game Purge 2022
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LMryIj-gt9A

A cull, itemised. Daniel (@dungeondive) walks through roughly two dozen games sold in a couple of weeks, giving each a brief cause of death. The hobby room is small, shelf space is the binding constraint, and roughly ninety per cent of his gaming is solo — so those two facts do most of the deciding.

Some go for being thin: Games Workshop's *Storm Vault*, a re-theme of an earlier Lord of the Rings game, shows everything it has in a single play. Some for format mismatch — *Fury of Dracula* is one-versus-many and he no longer plays those; *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Change is Constant* asks a solo player to plan four interlocking turns at once. Some for Kickstarter excess: *Siege of the Citadel* arrives years late as pure plastic bloat with bigger components and no better game.

The interesting failures are the ones he liked. *Chronicles of Drunagor* is a blast at the hero level and then locks its own contents behind an uninteresting campaign. *Adventure Tactics* reviewed well but is "just a skirmish game" in a big box. *Battle Stations 2E* has 20 pages of intro rules and roughly 500 of the real ones. *Hero Path*, memorably, "looks like Talisman by way of an educational toy store."

He closes trailing three martial-arts-film top tens.

----

What finally makes you sell a game you still admire — shelf space, play format, or something else?
